abstract: 1. The inverse coefficient of variation (/{sigma}) is widely used to quantify temporal invariability of ecosystem functioning. However, most studies have focused on aboveground biomass production, while belowground processes remain understudied. Minirhizotrons enable repeated observations of root dynamics, but the resulting data differ fundamentally in their temporal structure from measurements obtained through aboveground biomass harvests, sequential soil coring, or ingrowth cores. This raises questions about whether inverse CV estimates depend on the metric used to represent root dynamics and on when and how frequently observations are made. 2. Using a five-year minirhizotron dataset, we quantified the inverse CV from standing root abundance and two change-based metrics (net change and rate of change in standing root abundance). Standing root abundance was quantified from individual imaging sessions, whereas change-based metrics were derived from differences between successive sessions. We compared their inverse CV estimates using all 45 imaging sessions, monthly observations (n = 35), and annual observations (n = 5). For annual observations, we compared measurements taken before the aboveground biomass harvest and at peak root abundance. 3. Inverse CV estimates differed between standing root abundance and change-based metrics, and correlations were weak and often negative. Estimates also differed across measurement frequencies and timings, with responses depending on the underlying metric. Together, these results show that inverse CV estimates depend on how root dynamics are represented and sampled. 4. We propose that the inverse CV does not always represent invariability and that its interpretation depends on the metric used to represent root dynamics. For standing root abundance, it reflects pool invariability. For change-based metrics, we suggest interpreting it as directional consistency of root gains or losses. This distinction may extend to other ecosystem fluxes that can be positive and negative, such as carbon or energy fluxes. 5. Synthesis. Our findings challenge the assumption that applying the same formula (/{sigma}) ensures comparability and emphasize the need to align the underlying ecological questions and quantities when comparing invariability across ecosystem realms or studies.
